101.t: J. J. Johnson and Mark Brown Productions
101.s: J. J.'s versatility and his taking over the jingle office from Ernie Wilkins.
101.q: J. J. The stuff that this cat is made out of is unbelievable. He’s the type of person that could just stop doing this and start doing this and do it successfully. Get tired of it. Go do something else. He’s a great trombone player, great musician, great composer, great arranger. One time during the…

101.t: The jingle business and its money
101.s: Terry describes years of lucrative jingle sessions.
101.q: I’ve done so many. We did them day after day, one session after the other, and I – sometimes I don’t even know what they are. You just go and say [Terry sings a melody]. “Next.”

101.t: The studio routine: jingles by day, the Half Note by night
101.s: Hotel rooms near the studios because of daytime work and night club gigs.
101.q: Sometimes we would have to work – we went every day in the studio, Monday through Friday. We were finished at 7 or 8 o’clock with the studios. It’s a late afternoon

101.t: The Volkswagen commercial and Black jingle musicians
101.s: Ten musicians get out of a Volkswagen; Everett Barksdale and other Black players in the jingle business.
101.q: Oh yeah. We had a thing for – a jingle for Volkswagen. Ten of us got out of a Volkswagen playing When the Saints go marching in, something like that. Snooky was driving the Volkswagen. It just drove like “Vrrrrrrrrr” and stopped, and we got out, and everybody’s playing. It was just to show how…

101.t: How many musicians did the jingle work
101.s: About two hundred first-call players did nearly all of it.
101.q: In general, that same number – that same group of people who were on staff were generally the ones who were called – on first call of all – you see there were several contractors in town. One contractor couldn’t possibly handle all the jingles. So they had several people who were officiating in the…

101.t: A day in the 1960s: jingles, NBC, then the Half Note
101.s: A sample 24 hours of jingles, record dates, NBC from 4 to 7 and the club at night.
101.q: Oh yeah, yeah. You had to keep abreast of things, because a lot of times the jingle situation was really garbage music, so you had to do that in order to subsidize your yearn to play good jazz.

105.s: He composed and produced jingles for IBM, Revlon, Chrysler, Volkswagen and others.
105.q: Yeah. I was doing commercials. It was very successful. Very successful. As a matter of fact I would say during that part of the 60s some of the best music on television was the commercial music, because they were using jazz, a lot of jazz.

105.t: From Repulsion to his first jingle for Spring cigarettes and Ivory Soap
105.s: Mike Walman, who had heard Hamilton's Gerald McBoing-Boing theme, asked him to write a commercial; Hamilton became composer, arranger and producer, and wrote an Ivory Soap spot despite initial resistance when the agency learned he was black.
105.ch: The 1960s groups, Madison Avenue and film
105.q: Yeah. I’m there, we do the film. We close. Before we close I get a call from a creative art director from (Unintelligible) Advertising by the name of Mike Walman. He asked me would I do commercial for him and I had never done a commercial before in my life. I didn’t know what a commercial was but…

105.t: Wide World of Music: hustling the jobs, TV burnout, and the advertising crowd
105.s: He ran Wide World of Music with arranger Jimmy Cheatham, did all the hustling himself, started drinking martini lunches, and grew burned out repeating himself.
105.ch: The 1960s groups, Madison Avenue and film
105.q: Well I got burned out. TV can ruin you man. TV can suck all your talent, take all your talent. You know, for anybody to last on TV is amazing in a sense because man it can really burn you out, you know. I got to the point man where I would pigeonhole things. I was just doing things for money, which…

105.t: How jingle scoring worked, and a vocal bass idea lifted by others
105.s: He explains pre-scoring from a storyboard or phone call and says he originated a vocal-and-bass sound later used by Quincy Jones.
105.ch: The 1960s groups, Madison Avenue and film
105.q: Well first they had a storyboard, you know, the storyboard. They had it all laid out. A lot of times I would either pull score or pre-score, it didn’t matter to me. I could pre-score. I could make music from a phone call. You describe what’s happening, I’ll capture their action.

59.t: Jazz players moving into studio work, then back to jazz
59.s: Jazz players learned organ, arranging and conducting in studio work; the studio era later ended and they returned to jazz.
59.q: Well see a lot of us began playing jazz and then got into studio work, and were able to use some of that jazz expertise in one way or another in studio work. The improvisation for a pianist always came in very handy. And then the studio work taught us a lot of other things like in my case I began…

59.t: The New York studio scene and its players
59.s: Hyman lists the roughly two hundred studio musicians who did Kostelanetz, Percy Faith, rock and film dates.
59.q: Well yeah. Well now you’re getting into the studio scene in New York, which I was lucky enough to get into in the 1950s and stayed with into the 1980s. There were several hundred, as I estimate, it couldn’t have been more than maybe two hundred people who did most of the recording work in New York…

59.t: Cigarette ads and the firm with Frank Garisto
59.s: Hyman recalls commercial work for Herman Edel, then his own firm, and the strain of clients.
59.q: Well it was so long ago that some of them are now illicit. For example we used to do cigarette ads. I can’t remember them now. Too many products. When I was working with

59.t: Herman Edel and the client who rejected the music
59.s: A story of a client rejecting music in the studio, and the politics behind the control-room glass.
59.q: Well yeah. You get a storyboard and you come up with an idea and you try out the music on the client. One time I was working for Herman Edel Associates, Herman Edel that is, and we had a meeting with a client and we both thought we understood the client explicitly. We thought we knew exactly what…

717.t: The commercial studio scene of the sixties
717.s: Abene recalls one-ahead deadlines, Beatles-style sounds, the new generation of studio players and the education in writing for strings.
717.q: Oh yeah. 30’s and 60’s. I mean that was basically it. But you’d have so many meetings. I mean I had more meetings for the 30-second commercial than I’ve had for a record project. It was just nuts. But at the time the hip part about it is at the time that I was getting involved in the studio work it…

717.t: Music houses, demos and film scoring; no place to hang
717.s: He explains working in music houses with J.J. Johnson and Tommy Newsom, composing melodies, demos, post-scoring, and laments the loss of hangouts in New York.
717.q: Okay, I worked in a music house with this guy who started a music production company so he would basically write the melodies, he would show them to me and maybe I’d fix something here and there. And then I would orchestrate. So yeah, when I went to this other music house, which the staff was J.J.…

717.s: He recalls jingles for Fifth Dimension, Ella Fitzgerald with a Basie sound, Grady Tate and Vic Damone, and old reels.
717.q: Yeah but I haven’t done them in well over 20, well 25 years. But I did do stuff with the original Fifth Dimension for Chevrolet or Jello or something. Did some stuff with Ella Fitzgerald for McDonald’s was it? She did a whole thing but I did like a Basie kind of Ella thing. And then we did some…

1013.t: Mini-movies and decoding ad agency requests
1013.s: He scored mini-movies for famous directors and learned to interpret vague requests like a jazz track; funny studio anecdotes.
1013.q: Yeah they can be. I don’t feel that I was particularly a jingle composer, although I have written a couple that have been successful on that front. But mainly there was all the mini-movies with directors like Ridley Scott, Hugh Hudson, Alan Parker, John Frankenheimer, and then great photographers…

1013.t: Residuals and voiceover stars like Eartha Kitt and Mel Torme
1013.s: He earned healthy residuals; Eartha Kitt and Mel Torme appeared on commercials.
1013.q: Yeah. Residuals. Obviously they’re more short term because the campaigns don’t last years and years and years generally. But I always got a healthy residual for anything that I did write. Not as much as the voiceovers but —

1013.t: Writing 10 to 60 second spots; Elliott Lawrence; Tippett and Walton
1013.s: Very short spots demand tight focus; Elliott Lawrence brought New York work; he reused a campaign piece and adapted Walton when Tippett could not write 28 seconds.
1013.q: Well you really have to, you know, it’s a bit like the playing thing that I mentioned earlier. You have to pare your focus right down into that precise moment. I mean it is a very interesting thing to do, and particularly like there’s a lot for New York, and my contact was Elliott Lawrence. So…

940.t: Insisting on particular players and the power to say no
940.s: Rowe asks about Henry Mancini demanding players; Bergeron talks about alternates and the value of being able to say no.
940.q: If he wanted that, of course they would. I mean most of the time they’ve got alternates. They go, oh man, Plas Johnson can’t do this one, you know, but we have to do this today. Who’s your next choice? Who do you like? You know such-and-such sounds like Plas you know, or we’ll get Pete Christlieb…

940.t: Passing parts and the guaranteed double on film calls
940.s: Bergeron explains trumpet pay on film dates, the Los Angeles unwritten guaranteed double, and sharing hard parts with other players.
940.q: We do that. Not a lot. I mean on a film call it’s a little bit unethical because the money is very different from first trumpet to second trumpet.

940.t: Staying on composers' and contractors' lists
940.s: Rowe asks whether he can cut back; Bergeron says composers' lists keep him in the call and he just says he is unavailable.
940.q: If you did it a lot — but I think that most of the people I work for, because I always look at like there’s contractors and there’s composers and there’s orchestrators. And the orchestrators and the composers are actually more powerful than the contractors. Because many of them will have their list…

1036.s: Jingles were difficult but paid the bills while raising two boys, including a long run of commercials for Wegmans.
1036.q: Very difficult. Especially 60-second spots. You have to say it in 60 seconds but you also have to be able to cut that 60 down to 30 or a 20, or make it longer. I’ll say one thing, I should point out that all the time I was writing jazz with, you know, two young boys, two children and a wife, the…

1036.t: Residuals and union scale for studio players
1036.s: He and the players earned residuals when the union was strong; Steve Gadd did three sessions a day.
1036.q: I used to, yeah. When the union was strong in that realm and when synthesizers hadn’t taken over yet, yes. You’d get residuals for whatever the run was and if they re-used it you’d get residuals again. Yeah. And the players did too. That was a great source of income for players.

1036.s: Ad executives gave vague directions to impress clients, so he winked at the players and they played the same thing.
1036.q: Yeah. I mean anyone who’s done jingles has had that experience. Because they are there to look good to the client. And so they’re trying to impress the client with their knowledge. Because they’re charging them all this money. And all the guys in New York knew this. So I would go in and listen to…

974.t: A working week in New York and staying home for his kids
974.s: Leonhart describes his in-demand status, staying in New York for his children, and becoming busy on electric bass in the studios as sessions have declined.
974.q: Well, I certainly work a lot, and I know that a lot of people like me to play for them so yeah I guess it’s true. I mean I don’t want to be overly humble or anything, but at the same time I think it’s probably true.

974.t: TV shows, jingles and the 1985 Mazola upright bass commercial
974.s: He did TV and jingle work on electric bass; the 1985 Mazola commercial brought upright bass back into the mix, and he avoided Broadway pits.
974.q: T.V. shows and jingles. Lots of commercials. All those innocuous — Crest commercials and so forth and so on. A lot of them I did.

974.t: Playing with everybody in the New York studios
974.s: Being available in the studios let him work with nearly everyone, from Gerry Mulligan to Phil Woods, except a few like Miles Davis.
974.q: Yup, yup. Well being in New York and being in the studios, and being available, really available, I’ve had a chance to work with everybody. I mean just about everybody. I mean Miles Davis was one of the few I didn’t work with, I could name a small list of people who I never got a chance to play…

1004.t: Pepsi Pours It On and the commercial world
1004.s: She identifies the Pepsi jingle as hers and discusses its key changes.
1004.q: Well Pepsi goes up but it comes back, and by the time I go through the bridge it comes back down to the original key.

1004.t: Pepsi campaign lines and the writing competition
1004.s: Phillips tells how BBDO and Pepsi had writers compete for lines like Pepsi the generous one and Pepsi pours it on.
1004.q: Yes it sure did. Many deadlines loomed. But the funniest one really, Pepsi Cola, now they had [sings] come alive, you’re in Pepsi generation. Joanie Sommers singing a nice swinging tune. But it was the early ‘60s and the people that were getting married and having kids really didn’t grow up on that…

1004.s: Jim Jordan of BBDO asked for a jingle for a phone number; she wrote it on the drive in.
1004.q: Okay the first one is at 5:30 Jim Jordan, who was then the president of BBD and O but he had been a copywriter, the first copywriter to rise to the presidency. And I was doing a lot of stuff for him. And it was about 5:30 at night and I’m making dinner for the kids. And he says, “Anne, listen, the…

371.t: The closed circle of New York studio musicians
371.s: A select group of three or four hundred musicians did most of the work, fewer than a third jazz players; staff names including Specs Powell.
371.ch: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
371.q: Well, it was relatively difficult. You know, that is the person that I heard when I got to New York. They said it was one of the choice jobs in town and it was very difficult yet into. It was a small group of musicians. Most of them were also the musicians that also did the books of recording. They…

371.t: Balancing staff work with recording dates
371.s: Studio schedule left little sleep when recording dates came in; Milt Hinton and Bob Haggard's work.
371.ch: Hartwick and the CBS staff years
371.q: And being a jazz musician? It was difficult, it was not easy. Let's say you get a phone call to do a recording date, you have to schedule it. If you can do it at a time where it did not interfere with your studio work, your staff work, fine! If it did interfere, you couldn't do it. Even if you work…

371.t: Feeling like an outsider, and the nonstop recording schedule
371.s: Jones felt outside the inner circle yet recorded constantly; Teddie fielded calls from A&R men and contractors.
371.q: Not at all; not really. You see, I was still an outsider in a sense because I hadn't had the experience of working with groups like that. I had heard groups like that, but I was not what you would call an insider musically. I always felt like I was an outsider banging on the door saying, "Let me…

413.t: What 'studio musician' means; leaving Goodman for the studios and Lee Konitz
413.s: Maxwell defends studio work as an ethical need to support a family; Lee Konitz asks him for studio dates.
413.ch: Young players, schools and studio work
413.q: Well, it's kind of a put-down word. But studio musicians, it really is sort of a jack of all trades, but not necessarily master of none, because most of the studio musicians I know are the top players and many of them were the top jazz players. It was always a critical word.

413.s: Commercial transcription work paid well, before residuals.
413.q: In those days it was radio commercials or TV commercials, the background music that you hear behind the advertisements on the air. And in those days there were a great many, particularly before cigarette advertising was banned, half the work everyone did was for cigarette advertising, because all…

413.t: Ernesto, Larry, Freddie the Freeloader and Crip
413.q: Ernesto, yes. He was amazing. He was one of those wiry Italian guys. I think he was originally -- I think he had a shoeshine stand. And one of the guys used to leave his instruments by the shoeshine stand, I think it was Stanley Webb, or somebody like that, would leave them there. Then Ernesto…

458.t: How New York studio work came in
458.s: Work came by word of mouth and contractors; Beal worked for nearly everyone and usually knew little about a date beforehand.
458.ch: Studio work and learning the craft
458.q: It’s mostly word of mouth you know, but you do get hooked up with contractors who can depend on what you do because a lot of times they’ll book something and the requirements aren’t fully known and if you’re versatile, and they know you can cover a variety of styles and situations, you know, they…

458.s: Beal recalls forgotten jingle dates, residual checks every 13 weeks, union pension contributions, and McDonald's and Dial spots.
458.q: You remember some things but I swear to God like some commercials, you know jingles, you go in for one hour and you don’t even remember what it was, and you get residual checks for years. You know thousands of dollars perhaps. And you don’t even remember what the product was. It’s funny.

314.t: NARAS awards and being a studio pianist by choice
314.s: Bernhardt explains he was first or second call in New York studios, doing it to pay the mortgage and tuition while taking breaks for real music.
314.q: Yeah, that was in the days when I was pretty high up, first or second call on piano, on acoustic piano and electric piano in New York City, in the studios.

314.t: Studio call lists, arrangers and sight-reading dates
314.s: Taking time off never cost him work; he describes dates with Claus Ogerman, the Four Seasons, a film score with no piano part and Ennio Morricone.
314.q: I didn’t. I mean everybody said, “Oh they’ll forget about you the moment they call and you’re not there,” but I never had that problem. I don’t know. I’m glad I did it the way I did it.

987.s: Commercial dates like Maxwell House meant sight-reading and residual checks.
987.q: And one call could — if you get a Coca Cola commercial, I remember one of our successful ones was Maxwell House coffee. They made it into fifty different spots, then you get paid for each spot and if it runs longer than 13 weeks you would get a nice residual check. But you rarely knew what you were…

987.t: How studio calls worked: Radio Registry and the Sinatra date
987.s: Sessions were booked by answering service; Mike and Randy played on Sinatra's 'L.A. Is My Lady'.
987.q: Well that’s a tough question to answer because there were — every one was so different. But how do you get the call — it was a lot less dramatic than you think although let me insert this story because it’s a good one. We were just talking about this record the other night. Mike and I played on a…

1034.t: Ghosted rock bands and the Wrecking Crew
1034.s: After Rowe's Manny Albam story, he says studio players ghosted on rock records like the Byrds', Glen Campbell included.
1034.q: Yeah well the thing is there’s a lot of records of rock bands of the day — the Beatles played their own stuff of course, but there were some well known bands that were ghosted as they say. It was the Wrecking Crew in LA on a lot of pop and rock records that were supposed to be the band playing. I…

1034.t: Being a professional hired gun and the A team and Wrecking Crew
1034.s: Studio players stay professional whatever the music; he describes the competitive session scene, the Wrecking Crew, Nashville's A team and Hank Garland.
1034.q: You just have to be professional. You were hired guns and you were only as good as your last record that you were playing on. So it was very competitive. Everybody wanted to be a studio player and very few get through the keyhole. Especially back then. It’s not so that way — it’s almost a…

667.t: The Halo Shampoo jingle and a flood of residual checks
667.s: Rogers Brackett asks them to sing a jingle; they delay a trip and find the checks arriving in California.
667.q: You know in jazz you don’t make all that much money, and this is like what, oh, we couldn’t believe it. And for the few minutes that we were in the studio.

667.t: Roy's commercial production company and voiceovers
667.s: Roy produces commercials for Cheerios, Plymouth and Borden's, working with storyboards and timing, and gets voiceover work.
667.q: We did a car thing for Plymouth Automobile with Red Norvo actually, he was on the thing.

822.t: How studio calls worked: first call, second call
822.s: Answering services and call lists among George Young, Dave Tofani and Marini.
822.q: Well it used to be that we had a musicians’ answering service that the companies would call. But in the case of something like that I was probably called direct by either the writer or the producer who knew my playing and felt that I was appropriate for it. But there was a lot of times when you…

822.t: From recording musician to road musician
822.s: Scheduling around James Taylor and the Blues Brothers, the shift in his career, and the busy New York studio scene with Romeo Penque and Phil Bodner.
822.q: Only like James takes priority, and we know that usually we’re going to be playing in the beginning of the summer. And so I just sort of make sure that I have open space you know. But also, the business has changed so much now. You know for instance doing clinics. I did a bunch of them this year…

215.t: Contractors, midnight calls and Radio Registry
215.s: How session work was booked by contractors phoning at night and through the Radio Registry answering service.
215.q: Well they would call my house, say at midnight, and say we’re doing a date tomorrow at two, two to five. I’d say I’ll be there. A contractor would call me.

215.t: Why Bucky got the calls: rhythm guitar and the Doublemint commercial
215.s: Bucky says he was hired as a rhythm guitarist, unlike soloists such as Caiola and Mottola, follows Freddie Green and Barry Galbraith, and earns residuals from Doublemint and soap operas.
215.ch: Session stories and why he was hired
215.q: I don’t know, because I thought maybe because I played rhythm guitar, and there was always room on a recording session to play rhythm. And that’s what I was known for. Al Caiola and Tony Mottola were known for soloists. George Barnes as a soloist. If they didn’t need a soloist they wouldn’t hire…

444.t: How to prioritize reading a new chart; studio writers' personalities
444.s: Shew's order for scanning music (tempo, key, roadmap) and how he knew film and TV writers like Herrmann, Goldsmith and Peter Matz.
444.ch: Studio craft and the TV and rock dates
444.q: Hardly ever. Almost never. My wife could look at my face, the wrinkles in my face and tell whether I enjoyed myself or not. And she could tell. She said, “Another one, ey?” But I wanted to back up a little bit, Monk, if you don’t mind, just because there’s a thing about in the studio thing, it’s a…

444.t: Preparing to be eclectic; studio competition and cliques
444.s: Shew urges students to learn every style, then describes how fast word of a chipped note spreads and why he left the studios in 1982.
444.q: Well yeah but I think the thing is you have to learn to think on your feet you know. And I mean I encourage the students that study with me now, especially if they’re in school, I’m caught in between two realities on this. One of them is being eclectic and learning to play all styles while you’re…

933.t: Joey Levine and the jingle business
933.s: He became arranger for Joey Levine's jingles for fifteen years, dealt with ad 'suits' and later ran his own jingle company.
933.q: Yeah I got into the jingle business. And that was an interesting thing because a lot of guys wanted to do jingles because jingles the pay scale was really good, you were there for an hour and if the TV spot went national you make residuals, every 13 weeks you get a residual check, you know fifty…

933.t: Turning down work, session lengths and being as good as your last call
933.s: He explains declining some producers, three-hour bookings with overtime options and the fear of losing calls from contractors.
933.q: Not because of the kind of – I turned it down sometimes because if I didn’t like the producer or the arranger, if I thought they were like taskmasters or something that I didn’t agree with I would turn it down. Once I was established and was making enough money to say no, sometimes I would turn it…

532.t: Daily studio grind and reuse checks from R&B hits
532.s: He did record dates and The Tonight Show daily for twenty years; old R&B dates now bring reuse checks.
532.q: No when you’re working you’re just working. It’s just your work, it’s just what you do. I mean I was doing like I would get up in the morning and I’d go and I’d do a record date. And it could be the Jacksons or it could be Sarah Vaughan or it could be Barbra Streisand. I did pop records, I did jazz…

532.t: Craft versus soul in L.A. studio work
532.s: He felt studio work taught craft but did not nurture spirit, yet the unremarked R&B dates last.
532.q: Well there’s a union record of all of that stuff because it was all union work, so you fill out a contract, you know there’s a contract, it’s W-4 income with withholding and pension and all of that stuff if it’s union work. So that was good. But the whole time, all the time I’m doing all of these…

108.s: Jingles were his mainstay; the cool jazz Kent cigarette spot paid scale with no residuals; staff benefits.
108.q: That was basically what we were doing. But we were doing – we’d do record dates and jingles. My mainstay, really, at that time was doing television jingles. We used to do – at that time, the cigarette commercials were so popular. I did one with Buddy Weed. I think it was for Young and Rubicam. It…

108.t: Studio and network staff work at ABC
108.s: He worked seventeen years at ABC plus CBS and NBC, doing jingles and cigarette commercials, where classical training and sight-reading helped.
108.q: Oh, yeah. That’s what I used to do mainly. I worked for the American Broadcasting Company for seventeen years. And then during that period I also did a lot of work for CBS and NBC and we did a lot of recording work. I mean in fact, what I did most in my early years in New York was jingles and…

961.t: The Rice-a-Roni commercial and Don Specht
961.s: He played on a Rice-a-Roni jingle for about twenty years, written by Bud Powell-style pianist Don Specht, who hired top jazz players.
961.ch: Making a living: studio and odd work
961.q: It was actually a very good writer, a guy named Don Specht who was a jazz, a Bud Powell piano player. He could sit down and sound just like Bud Powell. But he, like a lot of guys, he’d gotten into writing jingles and he was good at it, and he always hired the hippest players — he’d have Shelly…

961.t: Craft versus art in studio playing and the late 60s decline of jazz
961.s: Studio dates meant playing with superb musicians and writers like Dave Grusin; he took it partly for survival during jazz's late-60s slump.
961.ch: Making a living: studio and odd work
961.q: Yeah. And that’s where the professional, again, yeah you’re absolutely right. There’s craft and there’s art as far as I’m concerned. It’s kind of like the old line, years ago someone said, “There’s music and there’s the music business.” And they’re very often two very different things. Yeah. On any…

408.t: Benny Carter's 1961 call and the New York studio scene
408.s: Woods explains why he was not busy in 1961, the new writers, studio scale, and recording with Manny Albam.
408.q: Well you’ve got to remember that I didn’t play flute so my studio work was limited in a sense. I mean I never did a Broadway show or that kind of thing. But you’ve also got to remember that the new writers were coming in at that point. We had Ralph Burns, Al Cohn, Brookmeyer, Manny Albam — oh the…

408.t: The New York studio scene and the flute he abandoned
408.s: Busy as a studio saxophonist among New York's arrangers; Jerome Richardson suggests a flute, which makes him faint.
408.ch: Studio years and the 1959 Europe tour
408.q: I got very busy in the studios, yeah, because all the arrangers were still in New York: Quincy was still in New York, Billy Byers, Elliot Lawrence, Al Cohn, uhh Manny Albam, Johnny Richards, ah the list is

506.t: Studio and commercial recording during the Miles years
506.s: Carter explains that Miles-band fame brought commercial and TV recording calls in a busy New York scene.
506.q: That came during the course of my time with Miles. At the time New York was bustling with recording. There were like twelve jazz labels or so. People from Japan would come all the time, they'd work with the musicians and then be off, and then there was just stuff to do. As my name became…

506.s: He explains the Suntory commercial that helped sell his Bach record and later spots.
506.q: Well, about thirty years ago or so, Suntory was … it goes way back. At that time, 1960 or so, the people who were in charge of those decisions in Japan came up during the war and they were all jazz fans because jazz was the big music in Japan at that time. As they got older, they maintained that…

376.t: After Shearing: freelance work, jingles and whistling
376.s: After Bluesette he became New York's go-to whistler for jingles such as John Glenn and Singer, and was on staff for the Jimmy Dean show.
376.q: Yeah. After I had done Bluesette, for instance, those jingles came in, you know, for the whistle. They said I was the known whistler in the studio scene in New York.
